core: Externality defined as a cost or benefit that falls on a third party outside a market exchange
Negative externality: private cost below social cost, so the market over-produces relative to the socially efficient quantity (market failure)
Positive externality: private benefit below social benefit, so the market under-produces relative to the socially efficient quantity
Internalizing externalities with Pigouvian taxes (negative) and subsidies (positive), attributed to Arthur Pigou
Command-and-control regulation as a direct policy remedy
Marketable permits / cap-and-trade as a market-oriented remedy
The Coase theorem: bargaining reaches an efficient outcome when property rights are clear and transaction costs are low, attributed to Ronald Coase
One worked example described in words: pollution damage of $100 per refrigerator shifting equilibrium from $650/45,000 to $700/40,000 units
supporting: Social cost = private cost + external cost; social benefit = private benefit + external benefit
The socially efficient (optimal) quantity vs the unregulated market quantity
Pollution charge as a tax on the quantity of pollution emitted
outOfScope: Public goods (non-excludable, non-rival) — a distinct market failure with its own topic; named and handed off
Taxes and subsidies as macroeconomic fiscal stabilization (fiscal-policy topic)
Monopoly as a separate source of market failure
Full welfare/deadweight-loss geometry beyond naming the efficient quantity

claims.claim: An externality is a cost or benefit from a market exchange that falls on a third party who is outside or external to the exchange; it can be negative (harmful) or positive (beneficial).

With a negative externality such as pollution, the firm's private cost omits the external damage, so social cost exceeds private cost and the unregulated market produces more than the socially efficient quantity — a market failure.

In OpenStax's refrigerator example, a market that ignores pollution reaches equilibrium at $650 and 45,000 units; adding a $100-per-unit external pollution cost shifts the supply curve up and moves equilibrium to $700 and 40,000 units, raising price and cutting quantity (and pollution). The price rises by only $50 because buyers and sellers share the burden.

With a positive externality, the private benefit captured by the decision-maker is smaller than the social benefit that spills over to third parties, so the market under-produces relative to the socially efficient quantity; innovation, education, and vaccination are standard examples.

Arthur Pigou, developing Alfred Marshall's idea in The Economics of Welfare (1920), argued that activities generating negative externalities should be taxed to discourage them and activities generating positive externalities should be subsidized; these are now called Pigovian (Pigouvian) taxes and subsidies.

Ronald Coase, in 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960), argued that when property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low, the affected parties can bargain to an efficient outcome on their own, and the efficient allocation does not depend on which party the law assigns the right to.

Command-and-control regulation specifies allowable quantities of pollution and may mandate specific pollution-control technologies; it improved air and water quality but offers no incentive to cut pollution below the standard and imposes uniform rules that ignore differences in firms' abatement costs.

A marketable-permit (cap-and-trade) program issues a fixed number of pollution permits that firms can buy and sell, so firms with low abatement costs cut pollution and sell permits to firms with high abatement costs, achieving the overall cap at lower total cost; the cap can be tightened over time.

A pollution charge is a tax imposed on the quantity of pollution a firm emits; a firm reduces emissions as long as its marginal cost of abatement is below the charge, so the tax leads firms to cut pollution where it is cheapest to do so.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which policy tool best internalizes externalities (taxes vs regulation vs permits vs bargaining) is a normative/policy question.
positions: Pigouvian taxes/subsidies set a price on the externality
Marketable permits fix the quantity and let the market price it
Coasean bargaining relies on clear property rights and low transaction costs
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the tools neutrally as options, explains the mechanism of each, and does not advocate a specific carbon or pollution policy, consistent with the subject's positive-vs-normative control.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 12.1: The Economics of Pollution
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the definitions of externality and negative externality, private cost vs social cost, the overproduction/market-failure mechanism, and the refrigerator worked example (equilibrium $650/45,000 units without pollution costs, shifting to $700/40,000 units once a $100-per-unit external cost is included). License verified as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; used as reference only with original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 12.2: Command-and-Control Regulation
sourceRecords.notes: Source for the definition of command-and-control regulation (laws specifying allowable pollution and mandated control technologies) and its three drawbacks: no incentive to go beyond the standard, inflexibility/uniformity across firms, and vulnerability to political loopholes. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 12.3: Market-Oriented Environmental Tools
sourceRecords.notes: Source for the three market-oriented tools: pollution charges (a tax on the quantity of pollution emitted), marketable permits (a fixed, tradable number of permits so abatement happens where it is cheapest), and the property-rights approach, which the chapter attributes to Ronald Coase using his railroad-and-farmer illustration. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Chapter 13: Positive Externalities and Public Goods (13.1 and chapter summary)
sourceRecords.notes: Source for positive externalities: the social benefit of an activity (e.g., new-technology innovation) exceeds the private benefit because of spillovers to third parties, so the private market under-invests/under-produces, and remedies include subsidies, R&D funding, and intellectual-property protection. Used for the private-benefit-vs-social-benefit mechanism; original prose.
